projects.title: The new Zapier: AI agents wired into 10,000 apps without wasting tokens
projects.what: Zapier CEO Wade Foster explains the Zapier refounding: your agent (Claude, ChatGPT...) does the thinking, and Zapier, through an MCP server (a standard plug that lets an AI use external tools), gives it hands to act in 10,000+ apps. In short: the agent is the brain, Zapier is the arm.
projects.how: A Zap starts when a real event happens (a new lead, a payment notification, the Monday report), runs the same steps every time and only calls AI for the steps that need judgment. A scheduled task in Claude or ChatGPT instead wakes the AI at fixed times to check for work, so you pay tokens even when there is nothing to do. Zapier's AI Workflow Index (2,944 real workflows priced) found scheduled agents cost an estimated 2.1x as much as Zaps. Zapier also says it fixes hosted workflows that break at 2am and recommends replacing AI with simple automation when AI is not needed.
projects.who: Ops people: separate what needs intelligence (writing, sorting, judging) from what is mechanical (triggering, copying, sending). Their advice: the next time you ask Claude for the same thing twice, have it build a Zap. Site not reachable, details limited to the tweet.
projects.try: Existing Zapier product, paid (pricing not read).

projects.title: A curator agent that watches a company's Notion knowledge base
projects.what: @StakeJein built a curator agent, hosted on LangChain, that monitors their Notion knowledge base, following a guide by Harrison Chase (LangChain CEO), who replied he wants to hear more.
projects.how: The tweet is truncated, so no architecture details. The idea of a curator agent: it regularly rereads the internal wiki to spot outdated, duplicate or inconsistent pages, and proposes or applies fixes.
projects.who: Team wikis rot quickly. An agent that gardens internal docs is a very concrete business case that is easy to reproduce.
projects.try: The LangChain guide is not identified in the truncated tweet; look up @StakeJein's original tweet.

projects.title: Rex (Superlogical): Mitchell Hashimoto's app lands on the App Store
projects.what: New iPhone app from Mitchell Hashimoto (creator of Terraform and Ghostty) that needs a Rex Server running on another device. swyx compares it to Cursor and T3 Code (beating them on day 0), so it is a tool to drive coding and coding agents from your phone.
projects.how: From Mitchell's replies: the app connects to your Rex Server (e.g. your computer), sometimes through Tailscale relays (a private network linking your devices wherever they are); it has installable skills, evals (automated tests of AI quality) and default rulesets (e.g. adding the Crush tool). They claim over 100,000 users and document all their external connections.
projects.who: Launching and watching your vibe coding sessions from your phone. Not yet available in France (encryption paperwork, submitted to Apple this week). Full public release said to be imminent.
projects.try: App Store (except France for now), Rex Server required. Price unknown. Site not reachable, details limited.

projects.title: A video game to learn Deep Agents, LangChain's agent harness
projects.what: @jess_weng18 made a video game that teaches you how to use Deep Agents, LangChain's open source harness (all the code around the model that gives it tools, memory, a plan and sub-agents), to celebrate its 50M downloads.
projects.how: You play, and the game hides educational content about how an agent works.
projects.who: Anyone who wants to understand what is under the hood of an agent without reading docs.

projects.title: Instructor 1.18: get clean structured data out of an LLM
projects.what: Python library: you describe the data you want (e.g. name and age) and Instructor makes the LLM answer in that format, validates it and retries if the answer is invalid.
projects.how: Version 1.18 fixes streaming, retries, batch jobs and provider integrations, adds classification and scoring through the OpenAI Decisions API and Jev, and makes raw response logging opt-in.
projects.who: Skip unless curious if you don't code in Python, but it is the base brick of many 'read an email, fill a CRM row' automations.
